The proposed listwise, reward-weighted objective is computationally simple, accommodates scalar rewards and pairwise preferences, and could remain useful as an empirical heuristic despite the theoretical issues.

The evaluation spans DNA design, protein inverse folding, and language modeling. The biological experiments report several reward and naturalness proxies over three seeds, and the paper includes informative ablations of sample count, regularization strength, and iterative relabeling.
The manuscript is generally well organized and provides task-specific hyperparameters in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central theory is incorrect. The optimizer of Eq. 9 is proportional to p_ref(x_0|x_t,c) exp(r(x_0,c)/beta_t). Equation 10 instead exponentiates hat r_t(x_t,c)=E[r(x_0,c)|x_t,c], which is constant with respect to x_0 and therefore cancels during normalization, leaving the reference posterior unchanged. Consequently, Theorem 4.1 does not establish the claimed equivalence between stepwise and trajectory alignment.

The proof contains additional consequential errors. Equations 22-23 drop the product of normalization factors Z_t, which generally cannot be discarded from a trajectory distribution. The derivation of Eq. 12 silently replaces exp(hat r_t(x_t,c)) with exp(r(x_0,c)), so the implemented empirical objective is not an estimator of the stated distribution-matching objective. Equation 45 also incorrectly places an extra exponential inside the sigmoid. These are not cosmetic mistakes because they break the paper's main justification for SDPO.

The experiments cannot compensate for the invalid central claim. DNA and protein baseline results are imported from prior work rather than established through controlled, matched runs, while the language experiment compares only against the unaligned base model and omits direct preference-optimization or other alignment baselines on the same LLaDA checkpoint. The claimed efficiency advantage is unsupported by matched wall-clock, memory, compute, or reward-query measurements.

Several conclusions are overstated. In the main protein table, SDPO has a lower success rate than DRAKES (75.5% versus 78.6%); the appendix presents a separately selected run with a different reward-quality tradeoff without a prespecified selection rule. Language gains are reported from apparently one run without uncertainty, and biological conclusions rely entirely on learned proxy predictors with no robustness analysis against reward exploitation.

Reproducibility is incomplete: there is no code release or algorithmic pseudocode, and important details such as evaluation sample counts, optimizer and scheduling choices, timestep sampling, model-selection protocol, and biological-task compute are missing. There are also inconsistent units for ATAC accuracy between the main and appendix tables.

The ethics statement asserts that there are no concerns despite applications to synthetic DNA/protein design and general model alignment. It does not discuss dual-use or biosecurity risks, reward-model exploitation, unsafe generated sequences, or safeguards, even though reward misspecification is acknowledged as a limitation.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering DNA design, protein inverse folding, and an 8B-parameter diffusion language model. The DNA results in particular show substantial gains over the reported baselines across both predicted activity and naturalness-related metrics.

The biological experiments employ separate fine-tuning and evaluation predictors, several complementary metrics, and three random seeds, which are valuable safeguards against simple reward overoptimization.
The ablations on sample count, regularization strength, and iterative labeling are informative, and the appendix provides major hyperparameters and additional protein results.
weaknesses: The central stepwise optimality derivation is mathematically incorrect. In Eq. 10, the quantity hat-r_t(x_t,c)=E[r(x_0,c)|x_t,c] is constant with respect to x_0. Consequently, its exponential cancels in the normalization and the claimed optimum is simply p_ref(x_0|x_t,c), contradicting the reward-dependent optimum of Eq. 9. The same problem affects Eq. 11 and Proposition 4.2, while Eq. 12 silently replaces hat-r_t with the sample-level reward r(x_0,c).

Theorem 4.1 and its proof do not establish the claimed equivalence to trajectory alignment. In the transition from Eqs. 22 to 23, the proof drops the factors 1/Z_t(x_t,c); these normalizers generally depend on the trajectory and cannot be absorbed into a global constant. Independently optimized per-step posteriors are also not shown to be mutually consistent with one joint trajectory distribution. Thus, the paper's principal theoretical contribution is unsupported.

The Monte Carlo derivation does not justify the implemented loss. Estimating each conditional partition function requires multiple x_0 samples from p_ref(x_0|x_t,c) for the same fixed x_t. Equations 12-13 instead normalize over pairs in which each x_0^(i) has its own independently corrupted x_t^(i), thereby mixing scores belonging to different conditional distributions. Proposition 4.3 analyzes the former estimator, not the latter training construction.

There is an additional algebraic error in Eq. 45: Eq. 44 simplifies to log sigma(tilde-r_w minus tilde-r_l), whereas Eq. 45 places an extra exponential inside the sigmoid. Calling the zero versus negative-infinity reward assignment the Bradley-Terry model is also imprecise.

The language-model experiment compares SDPO only with the unaligned reference model. It lacks standard post-training controls or competing diffusion-alignment methods, reports no multiple seeds or uncertainty, and therefore cannot attribute the modest GSM8K and IFEval gains specifically to the proposed decomposition.

The biological comparisons largely reuse numbers from prior work without reporting matched compute, tuning budgets, or evaluation sample counts. All improvements are measured through learned predictors rather than experimental validation, and the alternative protein runs in Table 9 are described as selected runs without a stated selection protocol or uncertainty.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of released implementation details for constructing the listwise batches and by missing runtime or memory comparisons, despite efficiency being a main claim. The ethics statement is also inadequate: it asserts that there are no concerns while presenting reward-directed DNA and protein design, without discussing biological dual use, reward-model exploitation, or safeguards.

The optimizer of Eq. 9 should be proportional to p_ref(x0|xt,c) exp(r(x0,c)/beta_t), whereas Eqs. 10 and 15 use the stepwise reward r_hat_t(xt,c), which is constant with respect to x0 and therefore cancels upon normalization, yielding the reference posterior. The proof of Theorem 4.1 also drops the product of state-dependent normalizers between Eqs. 22 and 23 and omits the required trajectory normalizer. The loss derivation changes objectives without justification: L_t uses exp(E[r(x0,c)|xt]), but Eq. 12 weights individual samples by exp(r(x0,c)). In general, exp(E[r]) is not E[exp(r)], so Proposition 4.3 does not establish convergence to the defined L_t. The pairwise derivation also incorrectly writes sigma(exp(reward margin)) in Eq. 45 instead of sigma(reward margin).

The derivation assumes clean samples are drawn from the reference-model posterior, but experiments use external biological datasets and UltraFeedback responses produced by other models. The impact of this proposal-distribution mismatch is neither analyzed nor corrected.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed contribution. The language-model study compares only against the unfinetuned checkpoint, without SFT, DPO, SimPO, or another discrete-diffusion alignment method trained on the same data. Biological baseline results are imported from prior work rather than obtained in a controlled comparison, and there is no ablation of the timestep weighting or comparison with straightforward reward-weighted denoising.
Claims of efficiency are not substantiated by runtime, memory, or compute comparisons; some configurations require up to 918 candidates per context plus iterative reward labeling.

Several conclusions are overstated. Protein SDPO improves predicted ddG but is worse than DRAKES in scRMSD and success rate in the main table. Language gains are modest, reported without repeated runs or uncertainty, and biological validation relies entirely on learned proxy predictors rather than experimental measurements.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no implementation is provided, and important details such as biological batch sizes, evaluation sample counts, timestep sampling, reward preprocessing, model-selection protocol, and full compute costs are missing.

The ethics statement dismisses concerns despite the dual-use implications of optimizing biologically active DNA and protein sequences and the known risk of reward-model exploitation. These issues require substantive discussion and safeguards.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, spanning DNA design, protein inverse folding, and an 8B-parameter diffusion language model. SDPO obtains strong proxy-reward results and generally retains reasonable naturalness or structural metrics.

The comparisons cover guidance, sequential Monte Carlo, diffusion-DPO, variance-reduced preference optimization, and RL-based methods. The paper also includes useful studies of beta, Monte Carlo sample count, dataset size, and iterative labeling.

weaknesses: The central trajectory-equivalence result is much weaker than advertised. Theorem 4.1 does not show equivalence for the natural endpoint reward r(x_0,c); it constructs a specialized trajectory reward after deriving the desired transition kernels. Because this reward depends on reference-model conditionals and intermediate states, the result is close to a reverse-engineered likelihood-ratio identity and does not establish that SDPO solves the original alignment problem posed in Section 4.1.

The theoretical guarantees do not apply to the implemented loss. The exact partition Z_theta^t(x_t,c,beta_t) requires samples from p_ref(x_0|x_t,c), whereas Eq. 10 normalizes over jointly sampled pairs having different x_t values. Consequently, this denominator does not converge to the required conditional partition even as N grows. The paper acknowledges bias but neither characterizes it nor establishes consistency of the resulting surrogate.

Proposition 4.2 implicitly assumes that a single shared model can exactly realize all target conditionals and attain zero KL simultaneously. Without an explicit realizability assumption, an argmin of the averaged KL need not match every target distribution, so the proposition as stated is false for a restricted neural model class.

The strongest biological results confound the proposed objective with iterative generation and reward relabeling, multiple training stages, changing beta and N, and—in the protein experiment—a changed reference checkpoint. A controlled comparison using identical data, labeling budgets, reference models, and tuning budgets is missing. The principal DNA improvement over DRAKES appears to rely heavily on iterative labeling rather than the nominally offline objective.

The efficiency and offline claims are inadequately supported. The best configurations use N as large as 918 and online-style rounds of model sampling and reward evaluation, yet no wall-clock time, memory use, total compute, or matched-cost comparison is reported.

Empirical claims are overstated. Biological validation relies entirely on learned predictors and computational proxies, with no experimental assay; in the main protein table SDPO improves predicted ddG but has lower structural success than DRAKES. The language-model study uses only one model, reports no seeds or uncertainty, and shows modest automatic-benchmark gains while omitting a comparison to the cited VRPO method designed for large diffusion language models.

The novelty relative to prior diffusion-DPO methods is not fully established: in the pairwise setting the practical objective reduces to the familiar logistic preference loss, while the arbitrary-N extension resembles standard listwise softmax distribution matching. No decisive ablation isolates the benefit of the claimed stepwise decomposition from these existing ingredients.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of code and missing details such as biological batch sizes, optimizers, evaluation sample counts, checkpoint-selection rules, and baseline tuning. The broader-impact discussion also fails to engage substantively with dual-use and biosafety risks from optimizing DNA and protein sequences.
